# Problem 1

### 1. Load and describe the data

```{r noaa_import, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)

data("ny_noaa")
noaa_df = ny_noaa

skimr::skim(noaa_df)

temp_count =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax) | !is.na(tmin)) |>
  summarize(n_stations = n_distinct(id))
```


The dataset contains `r nrow(noaa_df)` records and `r ncol(noaa_df)` variables from `r n_distinct(noaa_df$id)` weather stations in New York State, covering `r min(noaa_df$date)` to `r max(noaa_df$date)`. Each row is one station's daily weather record. The variables are station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and daily maximum and minimum temperatures. The data are already tidy, with one variable per column and one station-day per row. The original temperature units are tenths of a degree Celsius, and precipitation is in tenths of a millimeter; snowfall and snow depth are in millimeters.

Station IDs and dates have no missing values. Temperature data have the most missing values: `tmax` and `tmin` are missing in `r round(mean(is.na(noaa_df$tmax)) * 100, digits = 2)`% and `r round(mean(is.na(noaa_df$tmin)) * 100, digits = 2)`% of records. Only `r temp_count$n_stations` stations have at least one temperature observation. Precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth are missing in `r round(mean(is.na(noaa_df$prcp)) * 100, digits = 2)`%, `r round(mean(is.na(noaa_df$snow)) * 100, digits = 2)`%, and `r round(mean(is.na(noaa_df$snwd)) * 100, digits = 2)`%, respectively. Each analysis will use the available observations for the variables it needs.

### 2. Clean the dates, variable types, and units

```{r noaa_clean}
noaa_df =
  noaa_df |>
  mutate(date_parts = date) |>
  separate(date_parts, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-") |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    month = as.numeric(month),
    day = as.numeric(day),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10)

head(noaa_df)
```

I kept the original date and added separate numeric year, month, and day variables. The temperature columns were stored as text, so I converted them to numbers and divided by 10 to get degrees Celsius. I also divided precipitation by 10 to get millimeters. Snowfall and snow depth are already in millimeters, so I kept their units. The cleaning keeps all records and leaves missing values as NA; they will be handled separately for each analysis.

### 3. Most common snowfall values

```{r snow_count}
snow_freq =
  noaa_df |>
  drop_na(snow) |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n))

snow_zero =
  snow_freq |>
  filter(snow == 0)

head(snow_freq, 10) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Zero snowfall is the most common value, appearing in `r snow_zero$n` records. The next most common values are 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm. Most days have no recorded snowfall. These nonzero amounts correspond approximately to 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches, respectively. This pattern is consistent with snowfall recorded in inches and then converted and rounded to millimeters.

### 4. January and July average maximum temperatures

```{r monthly_tmax, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.asp = .5}
month_df =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
  mutate(month = case_match(month, 1 ~ "January", 7 ~ "July"))

month_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, color = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "January and July temperatures",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)")

jan_low =
  month_df |>
  filter(month == "January") |>
  arrange(mean_tmax) |>
  head(1)

july_low =
  month_df |>
  filter(month == "July") |>
  arrange(mean_tmax) |>
  head(1)

july_check =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(id == july_low$id, year == july_low$year, month == 7) |>
  summarize(
    days = n(),
    inverted = sum(tmax < tmin, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Each point represents one station's monthly average maximum temperature in one year, and each line connects the available yearly averages for that station. July is much warmer than January, while January station averages generally show more variation. The lowest January point is station `r jan_low$id` in `r jan_low$year`, with a mean of `r round(jan_low$mean_tmax, digits = 2)`°C; a low winter temperature alone does not establish a data error. An unusually low July point is station `r july_low$id` in `r july_low$year`, with a mean of `r round(july_low$mean_tmax, digits = 2)`°C. Its recorded maximum temperature is below the minimum temperature on `r july_check$inverted` of `r july_check$days` days, suggesting a data issue. I kept these points rather than changing the readings. Monthly means use the available temperatures, and lines can connect observed years across gaps, so coverage differences should be kept in mind.

### 5. Temperature relationship and snowfall distributions

```{r temp_snow, message = FALSE, fig.width = 12, fig.asp = .6}
temp_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily temperatures",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Records")

snow_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 13, 25, 51, 76, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall between 0 and 100 mm",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year")

temp_plot + snow_plot
```

Maximum and minimum temperatures have a strong positive relationship: days with higher minimum temperatures generally also have higher maximum temperatures. The hexagons show where observations are concentrated without plotting millions of overlapping points. A few extreme temperature combinations stand apart from the main pattern and may reflect data issues.
The snowfall distributions have broadly similar shapes across years. There is a broad concentration at smaller amounts, with additional peaks near 25, 51, and 76 mm. The relative heights of these peaks vary by year. The curves are smoothed density estimates; the exact most common values come from the frequency table above. The included observations are strictly greater than 0 and less than 100 mm, so these plots do not describe yearly snowfall totals or the frequency of snowfall.

# Problem 2

### 1. Import and inspect the data

```{r nhanes_import, message = FALSE}
covar_df =
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

accel_df =
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names()

skimr::skim(covar_df)

accel_df |>
  select(seqn, min1:min5) |>
  head()
```

The demographic file contains `r nrow(covar_df)` participants and `r ncol(covar_df)` variables: participant ID (`seqn`), sex, age, BMI, and education. Each row represents one person. I skipped the first four rows because they contain coding notes rather than participant records. BMI is missing for `r sum(is.na(covar_df$bmi))` participants, and education is missing for `r sum(is.na(covar_df$education))`; sex and age have no missing values.
The accelerometer file contains `r nrow(accel_df)` participant records and `r ncol(accel_df)` columns: an ID and `r ncol(accel_df) - 1` minute-level MIMS activity values for each person. The minute columns cover a 24-hour day starting at midnight. These activity data are currently in wide format and will be reshaped before analysis.

### 2. Select participants and label the categories

```{r nhanes_clean, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
demo_df =
  covar_df |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(sex, 1 ~ "Male", 2 ~ "Female"),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent",
                 "More than high school")))

head(demo_df)
```

I kept participants aged 21 or older with complete data for sex, age, BMI, and education. This leaves `r nrow(demo_df)` participants, excluding `r nrow(covar_df) - nrow(demo_df)` from the original sample. Sex and education are now factors with readable labels. Sex is labeled Male or Female, and the education levels are set to appear as Less than high school, High school equivalent, and More than high school in tables and plots. Age and BMI remain numeric, and all five demographic variables are kept. The original imported data are also unchanged.
